A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same inference-time hyper-scaling and Dynamic Memory Sparsification work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated or renumbered in v2.

before.justification: V1 reports original reasoning-benchmark evaluations, compression and eviction-policy ablations, and long-context experiments on Qwen and Llama models.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds Qwen3 benchmark evaluations, measured latency, and throughput results.

M1.justification: The operative DMS procedure retains learned eviction decisions, delayed removal, the distillation-plus-compression objective, and the same inference mechanism. Appendix C's separate-projection remark elaborates the already defined trainable projection rather than establishing a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: V2 retains the earlier benchmark coverage and adds MMLU-Pro, HumanEval, IFEval, and ArenaHard v0.1 in Table 2. This substantially broadens general-purpose evaluation, particularly by introducing instruction-following and conversation tasks.

E2.justification: Matched experiments retain the same vanilla, H2O, TOVA, Quest, and DMC comparators. Quest remains the cache-read comparator and TOVA the peak-memory comparator; the added throughput and Qwen3 comparisons use the existing vanilla baseline strategy.

E3.justification: V2 introduces measured H100 latency and throughput protocols, including throughput at the maximum batch size fitting each configuration. Added Qwen3 experiments use 32K training contexts, a 512-token eviction window, and compression up to 12×. Its Table 2 evaluation specifies a 131072-token generation limit, temperature 0.6, and top-p 0.95; these are protocols for added experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds controlled latency analyses across context lengths, model sizes, and batch sizes in Figure 4, substantially extending v1's analytical treatment of memory bottlenecks with hardware measurements. Figure 6 also extends per-head compression analysis to CR8. The original eviction-policy, data-efficiency, and context-extrapolation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V1 Table 4's unchanged uncertainty values are relabeled from standard deviations to standard errors in v2 Table 6. Appendix H.2 newly specifies averaging Qwen3 AIME results over 10 seeds and MATH-500 over three runs. This does not establish increased repetitions for retained experiments.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial latency, throughput, Qwen3 benchmark, and 32B CR8 results. The reported 32B DMS-versus-vanilla cache-read Pareto margins change from 9.1 to 12.0 on AIME, 7.6 to 8.6 on GPQA, and 9.6 to 9.7 on LiveCodeBench (v1 Table 5; v2 Table 8). These are revised aggregate findings, not demonstrated method-only gains under fixed configurations. Table 1 also changes DMS CR4 MMLU from 40.2 to 40.3.

T1.justification: The DMS mathematical construction, Pareto-margin definition, and latency derivation in Equations 2–6 remain substantively unchanged. Removing v1's standard multi-head-attention recap condenses background exposition rather than changing mathematical reasoning or theoretical results.

C1.justification: The abstract strengthens the numerical Qwen-R1 32B gain claims and explicitly associates them with equivalent memory reads. The central contributions—hyper-scaling through cache compression and data-efficient DMS with delayed eviction—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting measured latency thresholds to model scale and batch size, and compression gains to query-serving throughput. It removes v1's speculation that long-context improvements arise from mitigating over-squashing and lost-in-the-middle effects. Most existing limitations and mechanism explanations remain.

D1.justification: V2 Table 3 newly supplies model-specific learning rates and GPU-hours per compression increment, while Sections 5.1 and H.2 document the added measurement and sampling implementations. The checklist clarifies proprietary-data and incomplete-code limitations. Conversely, v1's specific 32B parallelism, checkpoint-storage, and total-project compute disclosures are removed.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for Qwen3, FlashAttention-2, and the four added benchmarks, while removing the over-squashing and lost-in-the-middle references with their associated speculation. The substantive positioning against DMC, training-free sparsification, and prior inference-time scaling remains stable.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: the original related-work section is split between Discussion and Appendix B, the self-attention primer is removed, and the results presentation is restructured. Detailed Llama discussion moves into the appendix, appendices are reorganized, and a conference checklist is appended.

P2.justification: The document changes from the largely two-column NVIDIA layout to a single-column NeurIPS format. Scaling plots are redesigned and redistributed between Figures 3 and 7, with compression-specific symbols and revised annotations. New latency, throughput, benchmark, and training-cost displays materially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: V1 supports runtime advantages mainly through cache proxies and idealized latency analysis; v2 adds measured H100 latency and throughput, substantially strengthening evidence for the paper's central practical claim. Broader general-purpose evaluations further test applicability. The gains outweigh the loss of some resource-accounting details, although throughput benefits are not universal—Table 7 reports a negative AIME margin for the 1.5B model—and reproducibility remains incomplete.
